what_its_for: Mitomycin is a chemotherapy medicine used to treat certain types of cancer. It is most commonly used for bladder cancer, stomach cancer, and some other cancers. It works by slowing down or stopping the growth of cancer cells in your body.
how_to_take: Mitomycin is NOT a pill you take at home. It is given to you by a doctor or nurse in a clinic or hospital. Depending on your type of cancer, it may be given directly into a vein (IV infusion) or placed directly into your bladder through a thin tube called a catheter. For bladder treatment, you will be asked to hold the medicine in your bladder for about 1 to 2 hours before urinating. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your body size, type of cancer, and overall health. Doses are usually given once every 6 to 8 weeks for IV treatment, or once a week for several weeks for bladder instillation. Never try to change your dose on your own. Your healthcare team will monitor you closely during treatment.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by a healthcare professional in a clinic, missed doses are handled by your care team. If you miss or need to reschedule an appointment, call your doctor's office as soon as possible. Do not try to double up on doses without talking to your doctor first.
storage: You will not store this medicine at home. It is prepared and stored by healthcare professionals in a clinic or hospital under controlled conditions. If you are given any supplies related to your treatment to take home, keep them out of reach of children and follow any specific storage instructions given to you by your pharmacist or nurse.
what_to_avoid: Avoid being around people who are sick or have infections, since mitomycin can weaken your immune system and make it harder to fight germs. Avoid live vaccines (like the flu nasal spray or shingles vaccine) while on treatment unless your doctor says it is okay. Avoid alcohol unless your doctor approves. Men and women should use reliable birth control during treatment and for several months after, as this drug can harm an unborn baby. Avoid breastfeeding while receiving this medicine. After bladder treatments, flush the toilet twice and wash your hands thoroughly to reduce exposure to others.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice: signs of infection such as fever over 100.4°F (38°C), chills, or unusual tiredness; unusual bruising or bleeding; blood in your urine or changes in urination; severe pain or burning when urinating; sores in your mouth; shortness of breath or coughing up blood; skin rash, redness, or blistering especially where the IV was placed; swelling of hands or feet; or any new or worsening symptoms. Also call your doctor if you notice signs of kidney problems like little or no urine output.
when_it_works: Mitomycin starts working right away in your body, but it may take several weeks or treatment cycles before you or your doctor notice results. Your doctor will use tests, scans, or other checkups to see how well the medicine is working for you. Be patient and keep all of your follow-up appointments.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do NOT use mitomycin if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. It can cause serious harm or birth defects. Both men and women should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 6 months after the last dose. Breastfeeding: Do not breastfeed while receiving this medicine, as it may pass into breast milk and harm your baby. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects and will be monitored closely by their doctor. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have any kidney or liver issues, as your dose may need to be adjusted.
